source.title: On the Limitations of Fractal Dimension as a Measure of Generalization
source.authors: Charlie B. Tan; Inés García-Redondo; Qi-Quan Wang; M. Bronstein; Anthea Monod

record.tranche_reason: The study explicitly reproduces a model-wise width sweep and measures evaluation accuracy, reporting double-descent behavior. It changes aspects of the original configuration.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 reports the width-sweep results and the text describes their shapes. Other experiments on PH-dimension/generalization-gap correlations and adversarial initialization do not test the listed double-descent versions. The paper cites double-descent findings from other work; those cited results are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: Section 6 reruns the Nakkiran et al. standard-CNN width sweep on CIFAR-100 (noiseless configuration) and reports test accuracy across widths. It reports a double-descent shape in test accuracy, which bears directly on V1. The setup differs from the original: no batch normalization, constant learning rate, and training capped at 250k iterations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report double descent in test accuracy and in Euclidean PH dimension, a monotonic generalization gap up to width 16, and that neither PH dimension tracks the gap. They treat this as a failure mode for PH-dimension generalization measures. They also suggest a link between convergence properties in the critical region and Euclidean PH dimension.
record.recipe_differences: The study explicitly reproduces model-wise double descent using a width sweep and evaluation accuracy, but uses CIFAR-100 and omits batch normalization and learning-rate decay to align with its chosen assumptions.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports a monotonic generalization gap in the critical width region even though evaluation accuracy shows double descent; loss-based PH dimension is unstable there and does not follow the double-descent pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: Euclidean PH dimension of the post-convergence trajectory shows double descent across width. Loss-based PH dimension does not, and is unstable in the critical region.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a CNN width sweep, Euclidean PH dimension tracks the test-accuracy double descent; loss-based PH dimension does not.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalization (accuracy) gap is monotonic up to width multiplier 16, even though test accuracy shows double descent there.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this CNN CIFAR-100 sweep, the train–test accuracy gap is monotonic across the double-descent critical region.

record.problems: The width-sweep result is presented as a figure rather than a numerical table; only three seeds are used, with standard deviation shaded. The text does not locate the accuracy peak relative to the training-set interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: Location of the peak relative to the width that just interpolates the training set (no training-error curve, and not all widths interpolate under the iteration cap). Other architectures and datasets. Label-noise settings.
Not tested: no test error over training epochs.
Not tested: sample size not varied.
Not tested: single deep CNN class only.
Not tested: label noise and regularization are not varied. Explicit regularization is omitted throughout.

record.verdict_notes: The double-descent experiment is a side analysis in a paper evaluating PH-dimension generalization measures. Because training was capped at 250k iterations and some widths did not reach 100% training accuracy, the interpolation threshold is not identified. The observed peak's relation to it cannot be checked. Peer-reviewed at NeurIPS 2024; code released.

versions.untested_parts: Tests one standard CNN on CIFAR-100 across width multipliers. It does not establish that the peak is near the size that just fits the training set, or test the pattern across other model families or settings.
The trajectory-sampling and post-convergence analyses do not measure test error over training epochs.
Training sample size is not varied near an interpolation threshold.
No comparison across model classes is made; the reported sweep concerns one CNN architecture.
The study does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study does not compare label-noise levels or regularization choices to test peak causes, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimal regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that changes the curve.
